starter.introTitle: Light up your first LED in 15 minutes
starter.introBody: No account carousel, no setup marathon. You'll pick a path now: real board on your desk or in-browser simulator. We handle the rest.
starter.introBullet1: You choose: real hardware or simulator.
starter.introBullet2: You build an LED circuit — we explain every line of code.
starter.introBullet3: At the end: +25 XP, 🔥-streak day 1 and a personal learning-path recommendation.
starter.chooseTitle: Do you have a microcontroller board on your desk?
starter.chooseBody: Either way — the circuit is the same. You can switch any time.
starter.chooseHardwareBody: We'll walk through 3 steps: plug in the board, wire LED + resistor, upload code.
starter.chooseSimulatorTitle: No — I want to see it first
starter.chooseSimulatorBody: Run the browser simulator. Hit "Run" — the virtual LED blinks. The code sits right next to it.
starter.chooseUnsureTitle: I don't know what a board is
starter.chooseUnsureBody: A microcontroller board is a small circuit board that switches power on its pins (e.g. ESP32 or Arduino). If you don't have one — pick the simulator. We'll recommend an affordable starter kit later.

hardware.step1Title: Plug the board in via USB
hardware.step1Body: Connect your ESP32 or Arduino board to your computer using the USB cable. A small LED on the board lights up — that's power, not our LED yet.
hardware.step1Hint: Tip: If nothing lights up, check the cable. Some USB cables only carry power, not data.
hardware.step2Body: Plug the resistor between pin D13 and the long leg of the LED. The short leg of the LED goes to GND. Order: D13 → resistor → LED+ → LED− → GND.
hardware.step2Hint: Mind polarity: the longer leg is the LED's plus. Wrong-way-round won't break it — it just won't light up.
hardware.step3Body: Open the Arduino IDE, copy the Blink sketch (you can see it next to the simulator), pick your board + port and click "Upload".
hardware.step3Hint: Once the upload finishes, your LED blinks once a second. Congrats — you just flashed real embedded code.

celebrate.title: You just built your first circuit!
celebrate.body: What you just did is embedded programming in 9 lines. Every bigger project starts the same way — smart home, robotics, IoT.
celebrate.toastBody: +25 XP for onboarding. Day 1 of many — come back tomorrow and it's two.
celebrate.repeatHint: You've completed this lesson. Pick a path now.

flash.title: Flash directly to your board
flash.subtitle: WebSerial · {chip} · one click — no Arduino IDE needed
flash.done: Success — your board is now running the sketch.
flash.doneBody: If the LED doesn't blink right away, press the RESET button briefly.
flash.errorHint: Common causes: wrong USB port, board in wrong mode (hold BOOT, then press RESET), or another program is holding the port.
flash.unsupportedBody: Direct flashing uses WebSerial, currently only in Chromium-based desktop browsers.
flash.unsupportedBullet3: Or: download the .bin and flash manually with esptool.py / Arduino IDE.

firstRun.s1Body: MicroLearn teaches you microelectronics — step by step. We start small: blink an LED. Then robots, sensors, web servers — your call.
firstRun.s2Body: Pick a board (an ESP32 is plenty to start), follow the lesson, and you'll have your first glowing project. Every step is small. Every step is explained.
firstRun.s3Body: To actually build something, you need a few parts from an electronics kit: ESP32, USB cable, LEDs, resistors. Each lesson tells you exactly what you need and where to get it.
